Introduction

Hi, I’m
Scott Shen.

I’m a junior at Marquette High School in Ballwin, Missouri. I want to work in public policy so I can help the people most affected by a decision have a say in how it gets made.

My school day tends to spill past the final bell. One afternoon I’m debating who should pay for health insurance. The next, I’m questioning a mock trial witness. Advocacy starts the same way for me in both rooms. Before I speak, I ask myself whose side of the story I’m missing.

Explore my philosophy

What guides me

My core values

Curiosity

I value curiosity because it pushes me to ask what a policy would change for the people living with it. In Policy Debate, I worked on a health insurance proposal. Changing the deductible percentage made me ask how much a family would have to pay out of pocket.

Advocacy

I believe one way to make society better is to help someone else’s concerns get heard. That’s why I take part in Speech and Debate and Mock Trial. Both give me practice listening to someone’s side of a story and making the strongest, fairest case I can for it.

Initiative

I value initiative because I want to find out whether an idea I’m excited about could actually work. My teammate and I wondered what it would take to turn an AP course into a role-playing adventure. Writing our DECA Start-Up Business Plan is how we’re working out an answer.

Philosophy

The gift of education

In fourth grade, I was playing with my LEGO tower. Green Goblin was halfway through wrecking it when my dad walked in and told me to study.

All these years later, I still remember how my dad described education. He called it a gift.

On this page

Follow the questionMake room for another answerPut it to work

Follow the question

When my debate partner and I wrote a health insurance proposal, economics helped me work out what a deductible would cost a family. My favorite question came from psychology. How would that family decide whether to see a doctor if they were worried about the bill? I want to study both sides of a policy decision.

Make room for another answer

Preparing both sides of a bill in Congressional Debate has a funny effect on my first opinion. Sometimes the argument I expected to beat is the one that makes me go back and read the bill again. I want to keep that habit, especially on topics I care about.

Put it to work

I want to become a lawyer. The part of Mock Trial that makes me want to do this for real is the follow-up question. I can prepare all week, but if a witness says something unexpected, I have to listen, set my notes aside, and find the question that helps the jury understand what happened.

Armstrong Teasdale internship

A summer behind the scenes

In summer 2026, the St. Louis Internship Program placed me in Records Management at Armstrong Teasdale. It gave me a first look at the work that happens long before anyone stands up in court.

Where a record goes

Mock Trial usually hands me a packet with everything in it. At Armstrong Teasdale, I learned about the systems that make it possible for someone to find the right record and trace how it got there. It changed the way I look at an organized case file.

Back at Marquette

When I prepare for debate now, I think about what happens if my partner needs to find the source behind a claim. Being able to explain a piece of evidence starts with being able to put a hand on it.

Looking ahead

My dream is to study economics at NYU. I’d love to study a subway fare increase in class and then hear from the people paying it on my ride home. I also want to become a lawyer and bring that training into public policy. I want to be able to sit down with someone, understand how a rule is affecting their life, and make the case for changing it.

Speech & Debate

Overview

I’m captain of Speech & Debate at Marquette, and I compete in Congressional Debate and Policy Debate. What I like about both is that I get to ask what a proposal would mean for the people it affects. That question follows me from school funding bills to health insurance debates.

Congressional Debate

In Congressional Debate, I spend a lot of time thinking about what fits into three minutes. One bill I worked on would fund cleaner public schools. Preparing both sides meant asking which problems a grant could actually fix for a teacher or a student.

Policy Debate

My partner and I developed a proposal for national catastrophic health insurance. The hardest line to write was the one about the deductible. Changing a percentage on our page changed what a family would have to pay. That’s the kind of detail that got me interested in public policy.

Mock Trial

In Dragons’ Bay, I prepared to cross-examine an engineering expert about a log flume incident. Which parts of the testimony came from firsthand observation? Which were inferences? I also earned Best Witness at Missouri Mock Trial in 2026. Sitting on both sides of the questioning is part of why I want to practice law.

Model United Nations

As a Model UN officer, I get to work on a different side of public speaking. Representing Sierra Leone on the Rohingya refugee crisis meant understanding the position of the country I represented before asking another delegate to work with me.

American Legion Oratorical Contest

I placed fourth in Missouri in the American Legion Oratorical Contest. Speaking about the Constitution pushes me to explain why a provision matters to someone who has never had to memorize it for class.

Future Business Leaders of America

As a vice president of Marquette FBLA, I’ve worked on chapter events and studied parliamentary procedure. I like the practical side of those rules. A member with an idea needs to know how to get it on the floor and how to call for a vote.

DECA

In Marketing Communications Series, I work through a business problem and present my recommendation to a judge. For the Start-Up Business Plan event, my teammate and I are writing a plan to sell schools and districts an educational role-playing game that teaches AP courses through gameplay.

National Honor Society

I was inducted into Marquette’s National Honor Society in 2026. Service is the part of that recognition I want to carry into my career, especially when someone needs help finding their way through an unfamiliar institution.

Science National Honor Society

I’m a member of Science National Honor Society at Marquette. What draws me to science is figuring out how to answer a question with evidence. I wondered what the word “natural” on a cleaner’s label could tell me about how well it worked. To explore that question, I compared tea tree oil with 70% isopropyl alcohol and looked at where bacteria grew and where they didn’t.

Science Bowl

I’m a Science Bowl co-captain. I like how differently a team has to listen here than in debate. A teammate might recognize the physics behind a question before I’ve even figured out what it’s asking.

Projects

Questions worth pursuing

These projects started with three very different questions. What does a community lose when a forest disappears? How well does a natural cleaner work? And could an AP lesson feel like a game instead of a quest?

On this page

Amazon rainforest researchThe efficacy of natural cleaning solutionsDECA Start-Up Business Plan

Amazon rainforest research

My paper, “The Cultural Effects of Deforestation in the Amazon Rainforest on Indigenous Tribes,” asked what forest loss means for the people who call the Amazon home. A map can show where trees disappeared. The question that stayed with me was what that map could tell us about the traditions tied to that land, and whose voices should guide conservation decisions.

The efficacy of natural cleaning solutions

I compared tea tree oil with 70% isopropyl alcohol to investigate how well each inhibited E. coli K-12 in a lab setting. I looked at the areas where bacteria did not grow around each sample. That gave me a specific way to evaluate a word I’d seen on so many product labels. What does “natural” tell me about how well a cleaner works?

DECA Start-Up Business Plan

My teammate and I are writing a business plan for a 3D educational role-playing game we would sell to schools and districts. Each AP course gets its own world, and each topic becomes a quest. We’d start with a four-lesson AP Psychology pilot. A teacher could send the class into a quest together, pause while students discuss what they noticed, and let them try the concept in the next encounter. That evening, their homework would pick up where the story left off.
